analysis.one_liner: Expands family planning funding, requires insurance plans to cover prescription contraception, and requires hospitals to offer emergency contraception to rape victims.
analysis.headline: The bill, introduced by the Senate Majority Leader with 34 cosponsors, was referred to the Senate health committee on January 4, 2007 and never received a hearing, vote, or floor action before the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The Prevention First Act was an omnibus women's health bill. It would have raised funding for Title X family planning clinics to $700 million, required health insurance plans that cover other prescription drugs to also cover prescription contraceptives, expanded Medicaid family planning coverage to more low-income women, required hospitals that take federal money to offer emergency contraception to sexual assault victims, funded teen pregnancy prevention grants, and required that any contraceptive information in federally funded sex education be medically accurate. It was referred to the Senate HELP committee and died there without any action.
analysis.who_benefits: Low- and moderate-income women who rely on Title X clinics or Medicaid for contraception; insured women whose plans excluded contraceptive coverage; survivors of sexual assault; and teenagers who would receive medically accurate sex education.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Low-income women and insured women seeking contraception

how_it_helps.text: Authorizes $700 million for Title X family planning grants for fiscal 2008, up from stagnant funding the bill's findings say fell 59% in real terms between 1980 and 2005 [S3].

Bars group and individual health plans from excluding or restricting contraceptive drugs, devices, and outpatient contraceptive services if the plan covers other prescription drugs and services, with cost-sharing no worse than for other drugs [S3].

Expands Medicaid family planning coverage to individuals who meet the income standards for pregnant women but are not pregnant, and lets states offer presumptive eligibility so women can get services without waiting for a full application [S3].

Conditions a hospital's federal funding on providing accurate information about emergency contraception and offering and providing it on request to sexual assault victims, regardless of ability to pay [S3].

Requires that any contraceptive information in federally funded sex education programs be medically accurate and include health benefits and failure rates, and creates grants for comprehensive sex education covering both abstinence and contraception [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Federal taxpayers fund the new appropriations; employers and health insurers bear the cost of adding contraceptive coverage to plans that already cover other prescriptions; hospitals that take federal funds must absorb the cost of providing emergency contraception.

drawbacks.text: The mandate applies to self-insured employer plans, so the bill's supporters' own findings concede coverage costs are shifted to employers and, ultimately, premium payers; opponents argued a federal contraceptive coverage mandate overrides employer and religious objections, and the bill includes no conscience exemption for objecting employers or providers [S3].
The Title X authorization ($700 million) and the teen pregnancy and sex education grants ('such sums as may be necessary') are new federal spending with no offsetting cuts [S3].

The hospital emergency contraception condition operates by cutting off all federal health funds to a noncompliant hospital, a blunt enforcement tool that objecting hospitals and religious institutions opposed [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefits reach a large, identifiable group: millions of low-income women who depend on Title X and Medicaid for contraception, and insured women paying out of pocket for prescriptions their plans excluded. The bill's own findings cite research that each Title X dollar saves $3.80 in public health spending and that family planning waivers saved governments money [S3]. The costs are real but modest: a mandate tied to coverage employers already provide, new appropriations, and the unresolved conflict with religious-objecting employers and hospitals. The strongest design objection — no conscience protections — is a fair one that contributed to the bill's political isolation, but the bill never got far enough for those fights to be worked through.

outcome.mechanism: It sat in the Senate HELP committee for two years — no hearing, no markup, no vote — and expired when the 110th Congress ended in January 2009.

narrative.text: Introduced January 4, 2007 by Sen. Harry Reid with 34 cosponsors (32 Democrats, 1 Independent, 1 Republican) [S4] [S5].
Read twice and referred the same day to the Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions [S5].
The only subsequent action in two years was a star print order on January 9, 2007; the committee never reported the bill and it never received a hearing, committee vote, or floor vote [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Health plans that would have been required to cover contraception, hospitals that would have had to offer emergency contraception to rape victims, and federal abstinence-only education funding streams were spared the bill's requirements. Women who relied on Title X clinics or lacked contraceptive coverage gained nothing.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Insurers, hospitals, and abstinence-only programs kept status quo

for.name: Harry Reid
for.what_they_did: Sponsored the bill and introduced it on the first day of the new Democratic-majority Congress.

for.what_they_did: Joined as original cosponsors at introduction.

for.name: 34 senators
for.what_they_did: Signed on as cosponsors — 32 Democrats, 1 Independent, 1 Republican.

against.name: Senate Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on January 4, 2007 and took no further action on it — no hearing, no markup, no vote — for the remaining two years of the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: Support was overwhelmingly Democratic (32 of 34 cosponsors) with one Republican and one Independent; no roll-call vote was ever taken, so no formal opposition record exists.

industries.industry: Health insurers and employer health plans
industries.note: Title II would bar plans from excluding contraceptive coverage when they cover other prescriptions, ending a common exclusion and shifting those costs to plans and premiums. The bill's failure preserved insurers' ability to exclude contraceptive benefits.

The bill would make abstinence-only programs ineligible for the new teen pregnancy prevention grants and require medically accurate contraceptive information in all federally funded sex education, threatening a funding stream these organizations depended on. Its death preserved that funding stream.

industries.industry: Title X family planning clinics and community health providers
industries.note: Clinics would have gained a sharply increased authorization ($700 million) and Medicaid family planning expansion, letting them serve more low-income patients. These providers' interests ran directly alongside the interests of the uninsured and low-income women they serve.

Hospitals taking federal funds would have had to offer emergency contraception to sexual assault victims without charge, a compliance cost for some institutions. Because the bill never advanced, no requirement was imposed.
